I feel like this is an artifact from Windows computing that users have taken for granted.

Even when you do a fresh Windows install, you must look for drivers and set up your machine. There's NO operating system, in the world (except for OSx) that will "just work" out of the box... and the only reason that OSx works out of the box is because Apple controls the hardware as well as the firmware... but if you install OSx onto a hackintosh, it becomes just as "out of the box" as every other OS out there.

But most Windows users don't realize this because the manufacturers do all of the tweaking, at the factory, before the computer is bought. The manufacturers find all of your drivers, set up all of your graphics, and configure all of your networking before you even buy the device (most of the time -- it's a "bad launch" when they don't). If you install a fresh version of Windows, you'll either need to do all of that yourself, or go to the manufacturer for their collection of settings/drivers.

This is evident with the Rasbperry Pi and Raspbian: You can buy a Pi and install Raspbian (a Debian form of Linux for the Pi) on it and it "just works out of the box" like you want. This is because the people at the Raspberry Pi Foundation have already configured Raspbian for that particular hardware. They've hammered out the networking, the sound, and the graphics for you. But there's no way that any OS maintainer can package your OS for every hardware permutation possible.

So, to answer your question: No, there's no version of Linux that will "just work out of the box." You'll always have to do some sort of configuration to make it work, just as you would for Windows. There are some that are easier to install with less configuration (such as Mint, ElementaryOS, or one of the Buntu distros) when compared to other distros (such as Arch, Gentoo, or LFS), but none of them are designed specifically for your specific machine.

You really ought to be top comment. I would even argue that Linux does a better job than Windows at "just working"; there is very little hardware that was designed for Linux or even with it in mind, so Linux/the community have had to do a bunch of extra work to make really any hardware work. If the situation was reversed right now, Windows would probably fail to work on 90%* of the hardware out there while Linux currently works on probably 75%* (without major user configuration) with 40-50% of that not having any manufacturer support of Linux.

*All percentages are made up based on my personal experiences with Linux & Windows.
